r: A pace plan treats the body like an engine that never changes, but the body actually runs on a fuel tank. A trained runner stores roughly 400 to 500 grams of glycogen in the muscles and liver, which covers about 2,000 calories. Marathon pace burns close to 100 calories per mile, so that reserve runs out near mile 20. After that, the body must rely on fat, which delivers ATP more slowly. A runner who banked a few early seconds on a cool, flat first half now finds the account overdrawn. Splits that felt sustainable at mile 12 demand power the fuel system can no longer release. Heat, dehydration that costs two percent of body mass, and eccentric quad damage make the shortfall worse. Then the wall arrives. To prevent it, run the second half faster than the first, take in 60 to 90 grams of carbohydrate per hour, and do long runs that train your body to burn fat before race day.
